name: Sky Steel
lede: Sky Steel is a muted blue-grey that our own library lists twice over: it is a color match, to 0 units of difference, for a second name, Bluish Steel Blue.

sections.title: One color, two names
sections.body:
Our library carries Sky Steel from a Japanese traditional-color source, listed there without a Western dictionary date; it also cross-references to Sora-iro, a Japanese name meaning "sky blue color" [1]. The ISCC-NBS system would place it in a vivid greenish blue block, about 5.6 units off that block's center, and the Munsell notation is 8.3B 5.5/6.0 [1].

In our own graph, Sky Steel is a duplicate at zero color difference of [[bluish-steel-blue]], meaning the two names in our library point to the same screen color [1]. The nearest distinct neighbor is [[beaucaire]], 3.9 units away, described as almost the same; [[dusty-steel-blue]] follows at 4.6, a touch bluer [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this blue-grey in 0.41 percent of 23,781 paintings, 97 of them, and the within-painting lens isolates it as a dominant area in 43, as photographed [2]. That ranks it rarer than 52 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 9 of 1,674 paintings, present in 0.5 percent of the 1,674 paintings (9 of them) dated to that century, 2.8 times its museums' baseline rate [2].

Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, 30 percent of its 43 appearances by lightness rank [2]. The earliest match in our archive is a 1467 panel by Marco Zoppo; our sources give no dated first record for the name itself, so no gap can be measured, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It is also over-represented in French painting, 2.5 times the expected rate, 18 of 3,443 French works [2]. In printed English the word "steel" (all senses, so this tracks the metal and the color together) rose fastest in the 1870s and has since kept climbing, peaking in the 2010s in Google's book scans [2].
